clinician.trajectory_summary: A 36-year-old male with a significant history of complicated diverticulitis (perforation, intra-abdominal abscess, colo-vesicular fistula) treated with loop colostomy several years prior presented with fever, dyspnea, productive cough with dark brown sputum, and epigastric pain. Physical examination revealed tachypnea, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and diminished right-sided breath sounds. Initial laboratory evaluation demonstrated elevated white blood cell count, total and direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and D-dimer, consistent with hepatic dysfunction and a thrombotic process. CT imaging of the abdomen, pelvis, and thorax revealed opacification of the hepatic vein indicative of thrombosis, a 9 cm hepatic abscess, and bilateral cavitary lung lesions consistent with septic pulmonary emboli. Blood cultures obtained on admission grew pan-susceptible Streptococcus anginosus. The hepatic abscess was drained by interventional radiology, and abscess cultures grew Escherichia coli, Streptococcus constellatus, and Fusobacterium necrophorum—organisms consistent with colonic flora, indicating an intra-abdominal source. The patient underwent serial thoracenteses and placement of a CT-guided drain for management of pulmonary fluid collections. Clinical status improved during hospitalization, and the patient was discharged on intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole for four weeks. The clinical presentation, imaging findings of hepatic vein thrombosis with septic pulmonary emboli, and polymicrobial abscess cultures from colonic flora organisms are consistent with hepatic vein pylephlebitis—septic thrombophlebitis of the hepatic venous system secondary to an intra-abdominal source related to his prior colostomy and fistula.
